title: Enums
summary: **Enums** are a TypeScript feature for giving friendly names to a set of related constant values — like `Direction.Up` instead of a bare `0` or `"UP"`. They come in *numeric* and *string* flavors, and a `const enum` variant that gets erased at compile time.

subtopics.title: Numeric enums
subtopics.explanation: A numeric enum maps named members to numbers. If you don't assign values, members auto-increment starting at 0 (or from the last explicit value). They compile to a real JavaScript object, so the names exist at runtime.
subtopics.example:
enum Direction { Up, Down, Left, Right }
const d: Direction = Direction.Up; // 0

subtopics.title: String enums
subtopics.explanation: A string enum assigns an explicit string to every member. There's no auto-increment, so each member must be given a value. String enums are more debuggable because the runtime value is the readable name, not an opaque number.

subtopics.title: Reverse mapping (numeric only)
subtopics.explanation: Numeric enums generate a two-way map: from name to value AND from value back to name. So Direction[0] returns 'Up'. This only works for numeric enums — string enums do NOT get reverse mappings.

subtopics.title: const enums
subtopics.explanation: Prefix with const (const enum) and TypeScript inlines each member's value at the call site and emits NO object. This removes runtime cost, but you lose reverse mapping and the ability to iterate the enum object — because there is no object left.
subtopics.example:
const enum Size { S = 1, M = 2 }
const x = Size.M; // compiles to: const x = 2;

subtopics.title: Runtime vs erased
subtopics.explanation: A regular enum is a runtime value — it becomes a JavaScript object you can iterate, log, and reverse-map. A const enum is purely compile-time: its values are inlined and nothing is emitted, so it's lighter but can't be inspected at runtime.
subtopics.example:
// regular enum -> object exists at runtime
// const enum -> erased, values inlined

subtopics.title: Enum vs union of literals
subtopics.explanation: Many teams prefer a union of string literals (type Status = 'active' | 'done') over enums. Unions have zero runtime footprint, work naturally with plain string values from APIs, and narrow cleanly — without enums' quirks (reverse mapping surprises, const-enum bundler issues).

subtopics.title: When to use enums
subtopics.explanation: Reach for an enum when you want a named, self-documenting set you can iterate at runtime, or to model a fixed domain (HTTP methods, app routes, permission levels). Prefer a string-literal union when you just need a closed set of allowed string values and want minimal runtime cost.

foundations.overview: Enums let you replace 'magic' numbers and loose strings with a named, documented set of related constants. Instead of remembering that 1 means 'active', you write Status.Active. TypeScript offers numeric enums, string enums, and the compile-time-only const enum, each with different runtime behavior.
foundations.formalDefinition: An enum is a named collection of related constant members. Numeric enums map members to auto-incrementing numbers and generate a reverse (value-to-name) mapping; string enums map members to explicit strings; const enums are fully inlined at compile time and emit no runtime object.
foundations.whyItMatters: Enums improve readability and prevent invalid values by constraining a variable to a known set. They're a common beginner interview topic because their runtime behavior — reverse mapping, the emitted object, and const-enum erasure — reveals whether you understand how TypeScript compiles to JavaScript.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a numeric enum as a labeled dial: each position has both a name and a number, and you can read it either way. A string enum is a labeled dial where each position's value is a readable word. A const enum is just a find-and-replace: the names vanish and their values are pasted in.
foundations.browserPerspective: A regular enum compiles to a JavaScript object (an IIFE that builds a two-way map for numeric enums), so it has a real runtime presence in the browser bundle. A const enum leaves no trace — its members are inlined as literals, so nothing ships.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Modeling fixed domains: HTTP methods, order statuses, log levels, user roles, and keyboard directions. APIs and configs often use enums (or string-literal unions) so values are validated and self-documenting.
foundations.businessImpact: Self-documenting constants reduce onboarding time and bugs from typos or mismatched magic values, which lowers defect rates in features like permissions and order workflows.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Enums centralize a domain's allowed values in one place, so adding or renaming a state is a single, type-checked change rather than a hunt-and-replace across string literals.
foundations.performanceImpact: Regular enums add a small object to the bundle. const enums add zero runtime cost (inlined), but can cause issues with isolatedModules/Babel and across module boundaries — many teams ban them for that reason.
commonUseCases: Replacing magic numbers in switch statements

commonMisconceptions.myth: String enums have reverse mapping like numeric enums.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only numeric enums generate value-to-name reverse mappings. String enums map name-to-value only — Status['ACTIVE'] is undefined.

commonMisconceptions.myth: const enums and regular enums behave the same at runtime.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A const enum is erased and inlined — no object is emitted, so you can't iterate it or reverse-map it. A regular enum exists as a real runtime object.

config.intro: Trace enum Direction { Up, Down } from declaration to its emitted runtime object.

steps.name: Declare members
steps.detail: enum Direction { Up, Down } lists named members with no explicit values.

steps.name: Auto-increment
steps.detail: TypeScript assigns Up = 0 and Down = 1, incrementing from zero.

steps.detail: It compiles to a JavaScript object: { Up: 0, Down: 1 } built inside an IIFE.

steps.name: Add reverse keys
steps.detail: For numeric enums it also writes { 0: 'Up', 1: 'Down' }, creating a two-way map.

steps.name: Use either direction
steps.detail: Now Direction.Up is 0 and Direction[0] is 'Up' — name-to-value and value-to-name both work.

interactiveExamples.title: Numeric enum and reverse mapping
interactiveExamples.explanation: Numeric members auto-increment from 0, and you can map a value back to its name.

sandbox.code:
enum Direction {
  Up,
  Down,
  Left,
  Right
}

console.log(Direction.Up);    // 0
console.log(Direction.Right); // 3
console.log(Direction[0]);    // 'Up' (reverse mapping)

interactiveExamples.title: String enum (no reverse mapping)
interactiveExamples.explanation: String enums hold readable values, but reverse lookup returns undefined.

sandbox.code:
enum Status {
  Active = 'ACTIVE',
  Done = 'DONE'
}

console.log(Status.Active);        // 'ACTIVE'
console.log(Status['ACTIVE']);     // undefined (no reverse map)
console.log(Object.keys(Status));  // ['Active', 'Done']

debuggingLab.title: Expecting reverse mapping on a string enum
debuggingLab.symptom: Looking up a string enum by its value returns undefined instead of the member name.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Reverse mapping (value-to-name) is only generated for NUMERIC enums. String enums map name-to-value only, so Status['ACTIVE'] is undefined. The developer assumed both enum kinds behave identically.
commonMistakes: Assuming string enums have reverse lookups like numeric ones.
Relying on enum internals instead of an explicit name lookup.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Get the member name from its value without relying on reverse mapping.

theory.question: What is an enum and what is the difference between numeric and string enums?
theory.directAnswer: An enum gives friendly names to a set of related constants. A numeric enum maps members to numbers that auto-increment from 0 and also generates a reverse (value-to-name) mapping. A string enum maps each member to an explicit string, has no auto-increment, and has no reverse mapping — but its runtime values are readable, which makes debugging easier.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A named set of constants; numeric enums use numbers (with a two-way map), string enums use explicit strings (one-way).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To replace magic numbers and loose strings with self-documenting, type-checked names tied to a closed set of values.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Numeric enums compile to a JS object with both name-to-value and value-to-name keys; string enums compile to a plain name-to-value object.

theory.whyImportant: Knowing the runtime differences (reverse mapping, emitted object) shows you understand how TypeScript compiles to JavaScript, a common beginner interview check.
theory.realWorldExample: An OrderStatus string enum ('PENDING' | 'SHIPPED') keeps API values readable in logs, while a numeric Direction enum is handy when you need both the number and the name.

nestedTopics.title: Auto-increment
nestedTopics.explanation: Numeric members without a value increment from the previous one (default start 0).

nestedTopics.title: Reverse mapping
nestedTopics.explanation: Only numeric enums map values back to names.

nestedTopics.title: Debuggability
nestedTopics.explanation: String enum values appear as readable names at runtime, unlike opaque numbers.

followUps.question: Do string enums auto-increment?
followUps.answer: No — every string enum member must be given an explicit value; there's nothing to increment from.

followUps.question: Why might numbers be harder to debug?
followUps.answer: A logged 2 doesn't tell you which state it is, whereas a string enum logs the readable name like 'SHIPPED'.

theory.question: What is a const enum and how does it differ from a regular enum at runtime?
theory.directAnswer: A const enum is inlined at compile time: each member reference is replaced by its literal value and no object is emitted. A regular enum compiles to a real JavaScript object that exists at runtime, so you can iterate it and (for numeric enums) reverse-map it. const enums have zero runtime cost but lose those capabilities and can cause issues with some bundlers/isolatedModules.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: const enum = compile-time-only enum whose values are inlined; regular enum = runtime object.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: const enums exist to remove the runtime object overhead when you only need the constant values.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler substitutes Size.M with its literal (e.g. 2) at each usage and emits nothing for the enum itself.

theory.whyImportant: It tests whether you understand the runtime-vs-erased distinction and the tradeoffs of using const enums in real builds.
theory.realWorldExample: A const enum for pixel sizes inlines the numbers into the bundle, avoiding a shipped lookup object in performance-sensitive code.

nestedTopics.title: Inlining
nestedTopics.explanation: Member references become literals at compile time.

nestedTopics.title: No iteration
nestedTopics.explanation: Because no object is emitted, you can't Object.keys a const enum.

nestedTopics.title: Bundler caveats
nestedTopics.explanation: const enums can break under isolatedModules or Babel, so many teams avoid them.

followUps.question: Can you reverse-map a const enum?
followUps.answer: No — there's no runtime object, so reverse mapping isn't available.

followUps.question: When would you avoid const enums?
followUps.answer: In projects using isolatedModules or Babel, or anywhere you need to iterate or reflect on the enum at runtime.

scenario.question: Your API returns status strings like 'active' and 'archived', and a teammate wants to model them. They reach for a numeric enum. What do you recommend and why?
scenario.directAnswer: Use a string-literal union (type Status = 'active' | 'archived') or, if you need a runtime object, a string enum. A numeric enum is a poor fit because the API sends strings, not numbers — numeric values wouldn't match the wire format, and reverse mapping isn't needed here. A union has zero runtime cost and matches the raw strings directly.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Choosing between a numeric enum, string enum, and string-literal union for API-driven values.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The data source (string-typed API) should drive the representation so values map 1:1 without conversion.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A string-literal union narrows a variable to the exact allowed strings with no emitted code; a string enum gives a named object if you also want a central reference.

scenario.whyImportant: Choosing the right representation avoids needless mapping code and runtime weight, and shows judgment about enums vs unions — a frequent real-world decision.

nestedTopics.title: Wire format match
nestedTopics.explanation: Prefer a representation whose values equal the API's actual strings.

nestedTopics.title: Zero-cost unions
nestedTopics.explanation: String-literal unions emit no runtime code at all.

followUps.question: When would you still pick a string enum here?
followUps.answer: When you also want a single named object to reference and iterate, e.g. to render all statuses in a dropdown.

coding.question: Given a numeric enum, write a function that returns all of its member NAMES (not values), correctly excluding the reverse-mapping keys.
coding.thoughtProcess: A numeric enum's runtime object contains BOTH name-to-value and value-to-name entries. If I just call Object.keys I'll get the names plus the numeric reverse keys. I need to filter out keys that are numeric strings, keeping only the real member names. Checking that the key is not a number (isNaN) does this cleanly.
coding.lineByLine: Object.keys(Direction) returns ['0','1','2','3','Up','Down','Left','Right'] because numeric enums add reverse-map keys. filter(k => isNaN(Number(k))) drops the numeric-string keys, leaving only the member names. For string enums this filter is harmless since their keys are never numeric.

alternativeApproaches.title: String enum (no filtering needed)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: String enums have no reverse keys, so Object.keys already returns only names.

followUps.question: Why does the numeric enum have extra keys?
followUps.answer: Numeric enums generate reverse mappings (value-to-name), so the runtime object contains both directions.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Enums centralize a domain's closed set of values (statuses, roles, log levels) in one module that the rest of the app imports. In larger codebases, teams often standardize on string-literal unions or string enums for API-facing values and reserve numeric enums for cases needing both name and number.
productionDeepDive.performance: Regular enums add a small lookup object to the bundle. const enums inline values for zero runtime cost but can break under isolatedModules/Babel; string-literal unions are the lightest (no emitted code). For most apps the difference is negligible.
productionDeepDive.security: Enums constrain values at compile time but don't validate runtime input. Data arriving from APIs or users must still be validated against the allowed set before being trusted as an enum/union member.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As a domain grows, a single enum or union definition makes adding or renaming a state one type-checked change. Exporting the set from a shared module keeps every consumer consistent.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Prefer string enums or string-literal unions for readability and stable serialization; avoid renumbering numeric enums (it silently changes persisted values). Document why a numeric enum is used when you choose one.
productionDeepDive.observability: String enum/union values appear as readable names in logs and error reports, making incidents easier to diagnose than opaque numbers. tsc --noEmit in CI catches invalid enum/union usage before deploy.

caseStudies.company: Large TypeScript codebases (e.g. many at Google/Microsoft scale)
caseStudies.problem: const enums broke under Babel/isolatedModules and numeric enums caused fragile serialization.
caseStudies.solution: Standardized on string-literal unions and string enums for API-facing and persisted values.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly less 'object-like' ergonomics vs. simpler, safer, zero/low-cost values.
caseStudies.lessons: Match the value representation to how the data is stored and transmitted, and prefer the lightest option that meets your runtime needs.

keyTakeaways: Enums give friendly names to a closed set of constants; numeric members auto-increment from 0, string members need explicit values.
Only numeric enums get reverse (value-to-name) mappings; string enums map name-to-value only.
Regular enums emit a runtime object you can iterate; const enums are inlined and erased, with zero runtime cost but no iteration or reverse mapping.
